course.description: How to replace the monthly FP&A grind with a repeatable Claude workflow. Covers setting up a Claude Project as your persistent FP&A workspace, loading planning models, spotting anomalies, updating forecasts, and running scenario analysis. Adapted from Wouter Born's LinkedIn post.
learningOutcomes: Apply the methods taught in Build a Monthly FP&A Planning System Inside Claude.

activities.title: Set Up a Claude Project as Your FP&A Workspace

lessons.content:
The foundation is a **Claude Project** that persists across months:

**Create the project:**
1. Go to Claude → Projects → Create New Project
2. Name it something like "Monthly FP&A — [Company Name]"
3. Set custom instructions that define Claude's role:

> "You are an FP&A analyst for [Company]. You work with our SaaS planning model which includes customer metrics, headcount planning, full P&L, and balance sheet. When analyzing data, always compare actuals to plan and prior period. Flag any variance >10% or >$50K. Use our standard KPI definitions: [list your KPIs]."

**Upload your planning model:**
- Your financial model (Excel/CSV) — the full planning model with assumptions, revenue build, headcount plan, and three-statement model
- Prior period actuals for comparison
- Budget/plan numbers for the current year
- Any KPI definitions or metric formulas

This project becomes your persistent FP&A workspace. Next month, you just update the actuals — the model and context stay put.

*Source: [Wouter Born's LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:share:7469334555737341952) and AI CFO Office newsletter*
lessons.title: Set Up a Claude Project as Your FP&A Workspace

lessons.content:
Each month, upload your new actuals and let Claude do the first-pass analysis:

**Upload the new data:**
- Current month GL export or financial statements
- Updated customer metrics (MRR, churn, new logos, expansion)
- Headcount actuals (new hires, departures, open roles)

**Ask Claude to spot anomalies against the plan:**

> "Compare these June actuals against our plan. Flag every line item where actuals deviate from plan by more than 10% or $25K. For each flag, tell me the dollar variance, percentage variance, and your best guess at the driver based on the data."

**What Claude surfaces:**
- Revenue lines that missed or beat plan
- Cost centers that overspent or underspent
- Customer metrics trending off-plan (churn spiking, expansion slowing)
- Headcount gaps — roles budgeted but unfilled, or unplanned hires

**The value:** This first-pass analysis used to take hours of spreadsheet work. Claude does it in minutes, and you spend your time investigating the flags rather than finding them.

*Source: [Wouter Born's AI CFO Office writeup](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:share:7469334555737341952)*
lessons.title: Load Actuals & Spot Anomalies

lessons.content:
With anomalies identified, update the rolling forecast:

**Prompt Claude with your adjustments:**

> "Based on June actuals and the variances we identified, update the forecast for July through December. Adjust these assumptions: [list specific changes — e.g., 'reduce new logo target from 15 to 12/month', 'increase cloud hosting by 15% starting August', 'delay 2 engineering hires to Q4']. Keep all other assumptions unchanged."

**What Claude produces:**
- Updated monthly P&L forecast for the remaining periods
- Revised full-year projections
- Impact summary showing how each assumption change affects the bottom line
- Updated cash flow forecast if your model includes one

**Best practice:** Make adjustments explicit. Don't say "update the forecast to reflect current trends" — that's too vague. Say exactly which assumptions to change and by how much. Claude executes precisely; your job is to decide the assumptions.

**Save the updated forecast** as a new file in the project so you have a version history: "Forecast_v3_June_Actuals.csv"

*Source: [Wouter Born's AI CFO Office writeup](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:share:7469334555737341952)*
lessons.title: Update the Forecast

lessons.content:
This is where Claude shines over traditional spreadsheets:

**Build scenarios in natural language:**

> "Run three scenarios for H2: (1) Base case — current forecast as-is. (2) Upside — new logo close rate improves 20%, expansion revenue +10%. (3) Downside — churn doubles, delay all non-essential hires, cut discretionary spend 25%. Show me the P&L impact of each and the cash runway difference."

**Sensitivity analysis:**

> "For our base case forecast, show me how EBITDA changes if: (a) revenue grows 5% slower, (b) headcount costs increase 10%, (c) both happen simultaneously. Present as a sensitivity table."

**What you get:**
- Side-by-side scenario comparison
- Key metric impact (revenue, EBITDA, cash, headcount)
- Break-even analysis across scenarios
- Sensitivity tables showing variable interactions

**Why this matters for the CFO:** You can answer board-level "what if" questions in minutes during a meeting, not days after. The scenarios are generated from your actual model with real numbers — not back-of-napkin estimates.

*Source: [Wouter Born's AI CFO Office writeup](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:share:7469334555737341952)*
lessons.title: Run Scenarios with Sensitivity Analysis

activities.title: Save the Workflow for Next Month

lessons.content:
The biggest payoff: next month takes half the time.

**What persists in your Claude Project:**
- Your planning model and all assumptions
- Custom instructions and analysis preferences
- Previous forecasts and scenario outputs
- The conversation history showing your analysis patterns

**Monthly workflow (after first setup):**
1. Upload new month's actuals (5 min)
2. Ask Claude to run the anomaly analysis (2 min to generate, 15 min to review)
3. Decide on assumption changes based on findings (your judgment)
4. Update the forecast with new assumptions (2 min)
5. Run any requested scenarios (2 min each)
6. Export deliverables for the board/leadership

**Total time:** What used to be a multi-day FP&A cycle becomes a focused 2-3 hour session — and most of that time is your decision-making, not data manipulation.

**Pro tip:** At the end of each month's session, ask Claude: "Summarize the key decisions and assumption changes we made this month. Save this as a decision log." Over time, you build an audit trail of forecast evolution that's invaluable for board discussions.

*Source: [Wouter Born's LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:share:7469334555737341952) — full writeup shared with 45,000+ CFOs at AI CFO Office*
